metadata.title: The Trump Phone Is More Novelty Than Serious Smartphone Contender

content.text:
(Bloomberg) -- The Trump phone is finally here — sort of — and it bears little resemblance to the original pitch.
Most Read from Bloomberg
First introduced a year ago at Trump Tower by President Donald Trump's eldest sons, the T1 from Trump Mobile was touted as a gold-colored handset with a faint iPhone resemblance that would be proudly made in the US, even though modern manufacturing realities made that impossible.
Fast forward to today, and the actual $499 product is a repurposed Android phone first released by HTC, a Taiwanese brand, two years ago. It's absolutely not made stateside, and the hardware looks nothing like the initial design. And so far, there's little evidence that Trump Mobile is actually shipping the T1 to customers at any significant volume. Only a few media outlets have received sample units, leaving open the possibility that this could be a doomed business venture.
Taken on its own merits, the T1 phone itself is better than some might expect: It has a larger screen than Apple Inc.'s iPhone 17e and other hardware specifications that make the asking price fairly reasonable. By most criteria, it's in the same ballpark as other midrange Android devices. This phone isn't junk, but there are glaring weaknesses, like the camera, and far too much uncertainty around long-term support and Trump Mobile itself to recommend the T1 to anyone, even Trump's biggest fans.
Hardware
In the shipment box, I found a Trump Mobile SIM card, a user manual and a "Quick Start guide" on a one-sided sheet of paper that looked like it came straight out of an office printer. As for the phone's packaging, it's a no-frills black box with Trump Mobile embossed on the front, a T1 logo on the bottom, and another Trump Mobile logo around back, this one with an American flag.
Trump Mobile includes a clear case for the T1, a USB-C cable and a 30-watt wall charger. That's a bonus nowadays: You won't find chargers bundled with most smartphones from major brands.
Turning to the T1 itself, its finish often looks more mustard yellow than "gold," but the overall hardware is a perfectly acceptable Android phone. A teardown by iFixit found the device to be a near-perfect match for HTC's U24 Pro, which went on sale in mid-2024. Like that device, the T1 is powered by a Qualcomm Inc. Snapdragon 7 Gen 3 processor and contains 512 gigabytes of storage and 12 gigabytes of memory. Credit where it's due, these specifications aren't bad.
There's a built-in headphone jack, and the T1 also supports microSD cards if you want to add more space for media and files. Older HTC handsets were often lauded for the audio quality of their headphone connector, but this one is purely average, avoiding a scenario where the Trump phone might have somehow caught the attention of audiophiles.
The T1 has a 6.78-inch OLED screen that curves at the sides, a once-popular trend among Android manufacturers that's less common today. The display itself is crisp and colorful, with a fluid 120-hertz refresh rate. But it doesn't get nearly as bright as the latest similarly priced phones from Alphabet Inc.'s Google, Samsung Electronics Co. or Nothing Technologies Ltd.
The device runs Android 15 out of the box with barely any customization or software tweaks. There's a Trump Mobile loading animation, and Truth Social, President Trump's social media platform, comes preinstalled. (So does a telehealth app called Doctegrity, strangely enough.) Beyond that, you are left with the usual smattering of Google apps and can install other software from the Play Store like on any Android product.
But most Android manufacturers have a proven track record when it comes to providing software updates and security patches. The majority of this phone's competitors have already upgraded to Android 16 (and 17 is now rolling out). Long-term support is a complete unknown with the T1. It's currently stuck on a February 2026 security update, and it's unclear if Trump Mobile will provide regular updates to safeguard the device from the latest vulnerabilities.
Camera Performance
Like the HTC phone, the T1 has a triple-lens rear camera array with a 50-megapixel main sensor, 50-megapixel zoom lens, and 8-megapixel ultra-wide camera. The primary lens is serviceable outdoors in good light, but it struggled indoors when I took some test shots at Trump Tower.
What's more, shutter lag can ruin photos and cause blur if you're not mindful about holding still, and the T1's very basic image processing is several generations behind the computational enhancements that make it easy to shoot from the hip with other handsets. In a dimly lit restaurant, my food photos were underwhelming.
The camera app also offers no explanation for what buttons like "AI" do, even if I'm fairly sure it's scene recognition in this case. But there's an icon of a star inside a circle that I remain clueless about to this day. You can apply an optional watermark to images captured with the T1 to make it crystal clear what phone you're using, though this is disabled by default.
Trump Mobile's 47 Plan
Trump Mobile is a mobile virtual network operator, or MVNO, that is powered by Florida-based Liberty Mobile Wireless, which itself operates on T-Mobile US Inc.'s cellular network. Coverage and data speeds should be on par with what you'd get from T-Mobile or other carriers that piggyback on it.
But Trump Mobile's $47.45 monthly rate — a nod to Donald Trump's two terms in office — isn't a good value compared with Visible, Google Fi, US Mobile, Mint Mobile and other providers in the fiercely competitive prepaid market. I currently pay Visible $35 per month for unlimited data and high-speed hot spot connectivity, and that includes bundled service for my smartwatch at no extra charge.
Trump Mobile offers perks such as roadside assistance and telehealth coverage, and "Trump" will appear in your phone's status bar when connected to the network. But I'd never switch to this provider from a more established carrier. Rival services have mobile apps where you can monitor your data usage or adjust account settings. They're continually offering new discounts and freebies to keep you as a customer.
There's none of this with Trump Mobile, and the customer service operation seems to be extremely limited: Live operators are only available between 8 a.m. and 11 p.m. Central Time. The agents I've interacted with so far have been very kind, but that's not enough to sway me.
It's important to understand that, per the fine print on its own website, Trump Mobile has no direct affiliation with the Trump Organization. Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. were part of the product unveiling and early publicity, but that seems to be where their involvement ends.
Is the T1 Actually Real?
Technically, the Trump Mobile T1 exists. I've been using one for a couple weeks now. But there's a lot of skepticism around the idea that this handset will ever ship in volume to the ardent President Trump supporters who backed it. Regardless, the T1 I have in my hands is drastically different from what was promised a year ago. Trump Mobile now claims the hardware is partially "assembled" in the US, but it's unclear what that refers to at this point.
No matter what side of the political aisle you're on, you'd be better off with alternatives like Google's Pixel 10a, the iPhone 17e or a wide range of mid-tier options from Samsung and Lenovo Group Ltd.'s Motorola. It's easy to find a better phone than this in 2026, and if President Trump himself isn't going to use the T1 phone daily, why should you?
